title: Spectral Graph Theory Glossary
description: Spectral graph theory vocabulary used in the project, covering the spectrum of the graph Laplacian, diffusion, random-walk behavior, density of states, and spectral dimension — all central diagnostics of multi-sheeted tilings.

adjacency-matrix.summary: The n×n symmetric matrix with A_ij = 1 if vertices i and j are adjacent, else 0.
adjacency-matrix.definition:
The $n \times n$ matrix with $A_{ij} = 1$ if vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent, else 0.

For undirected graphs (the project's focus): $A$ is **symmetric**, hence has real eigenvalues. The largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}(A)$ controls the rate of exponential growth of walk counts. The full spectrum encodes detailed structural information.

formulas.description: Entry definition of the adjacency matrix.

variables.A_{ij}: Entry in row i, column j of the adjacency matrix
variables.i \\sim j: Vertices i and j are adjacent

degree-matrix.summary: The diagonal matrix with D_ii equal to the degree (number of neighbors) of vertex v_i.
degree-matrix.definition:
The diagonal matrix with $D_{ii} = \deg(v_i)$ = number of neighbors of vertex $v_i$.

All off-diagonal entries are zero. The degree matrix is used together with the adjacency matrix to construct the graph Laplacian.

formulas.description: Diagonal entry of the degree matrix equals the degree of vertex v_i.

variables.\\deg(v_i): Number of neighbors of vertex v_i

graph-laplacian.summary: The discrete analogue of the Laplace operator, defined as Δ = D − A, encoding diffusion and connectivity of a graph.
graph-laplacian.definition:
The **discrete analogue of the Laplace operator**, defined as $\Delta = D - A$:

$$(\Delta f)(v) = \sum_{u \sim v} \big(f(v) - f(u)\big) = \deg(v) f(v) - \sum_{u \sim v} f(u)$$

**Properties:**

- Symmetric (for undirected graphs).
- Positive semi-definite: all eigenvalues $\geq 0$.
- $\Delta \mathbf{1} = 0$: constants are in the kernel.
- The **multiplicity of eigenvalue 0** equals the number of connected components.

examples.title: Path graph P_3
examples.body:
For a path graph on 3 vertices (1–2–3), the Laplacian is:

Δ = [[1, -1, 0], [-1, 2, -1], [0, -1, 1]]

Eigenvalues: 0, 1, 3. The single zero eigenvalue confirms the graph is connected.

formulas.description: Graph Laplacian as the difference of degree matrix and adjacency matrix.
Action of the graph Laplacian on a function f defined on vertices.

sparse-matrix.summary: A matrix with O(n) non-zero entries rather than O(n²), enabling efficient algorithms for large graphs.
sparse-matrix.definition: A matrix with $O(n)$ non-zero entries (rather than $O(n^2)$). The adjacency matrix of a graph with bounded degree is automatically sparse. **Sparse linear algebra** algorithms (Lanczos, Arnoldi, conjugate gradient) exploit sparsity for efficiency.

examples.title: Bounded-degree graph adjacency matrix
examples.body: For a graph where every vertex has at most d neighbors, the adjacency matrix has at most n·d non-zero entries. For d fixed and n large, this is O(n) rather than O(n²), making matrix-vector products O(n) instead of O(n²).

sparse-linear-algebra.summary: Algorithms designed for sparse matrices that exploit O(n) non-zero structure for efficient matrix-vector products and iterative eigensolvers.
sparse-linear-algebra.definition:
Algorithms designed for sparse matrices. Standard for large graphs:

- **Matrix-vector products** are $O(n)$ instead of $O(n^2)$.
- **Iterative eigensolvers** (Lanczos, Arnoldi) avoid forming the full eigendecomposition.
- **Shift-invert** transformations access specific spectral ranges.

eigenvalue.summary: A scalar λ such that Mv = λv for some non-zero eigenvector v.
eigenvalue.definition:
A scalar $\lambda$ such that $Mv = \lambda v$ for some non-zero **eigenvector** $v$.

For symmetric matrices (such as the graph Laplacian), all eigenvalues are real. The collection of all eigenvalues forms the **spectrum** of the matrix.

formulas.description: Eigenvalue equation: M acts on eigenvector v by scaling it by λ.

spectrum.summary: The set (or multiset) of eigenvalues of a matrix or operator; for the graph Laplacian, all eigenvalues are non-negative.
spectrum.definition:
The **set (or multiset) of eigenvalues** of a matrix or operator. For the graph Laplacian:

$$0 = \lambda_0 \leq \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$$

The spectrum encodes structural information about the graph, including connectivity (multiplicity of zero), mixing properties (spectral gap), and diffusion behavior (density of states).

formulas.description: Ordered spectrum of the graph Laplacian, with all eigenvalues non-negative.

variables.\\lambda_i: i-th eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian in non-decreasing order

spectral-gap.summary: The smallest non-zero Laplacian eigenvalue λ₁, controlling random-walk mixing time and graph connectivity.
spectral-gap.definition:
The **smallest non-zero Laplacian eigenvalue**, $\lambda_1$.

- $\lambda_1 = 0$: graph is disconnected.
- Large $\lambda_1$: graph is well-connected, "expander-like."
- $\lambda_1 \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$: typical for graphs that "look low-dimensional."

The spectral gap controls **mixing time** of random walks and the **isoperimetric** properties of the graph.

examples.title: Expander vs. lattice
examples.body: For a d-regular expander graph, λ₁ ≥ c > 0 uniformly as n → ∞, giving O(log n) mixing time. For the integer lattice ℤ^d restricted to an n-vertex ball, λ₁ ~ n^{-2/d} → 0, reflecting slow polynomial mixing.

formulas.description: Mixing time of a random walk is inversely proportional to the spectral gap.

cheeger-constant.summary: The graph isoperimetric ratio h(G) measuring the minimum edge boundary relative to set size, related to the spectral gap by Cheeger's inequality.
cheeger-constant.definition:
The **graph isoperimetric ratio**:

$$h(G) = \min_S \frac{|\partial S|}{\min(|S|, |V \setminus S|)}$$

where $\partial S$ is the edge boundary. **Cheeger's inequality** relates it to the spectral gap:

$$\frac{h(G)^2}{2 d_{\max}} \leq \lambda_1 \leq 2 h(G)$$

A small Cheeger constant indicates a **bottleneck**; the corresponding small $\lambda_1$ reflects slow mixing.

examples.title: Dumbbell graph
examples.body: A graph consisting of two cliques connected by a single edge has h(G) = 1/n (one edge boundary, sets of size ~n/2). This small Cheeger constant signals a bottleneck and corresponds to a near-zero spectral gap λ₁ ~ 1/n².

formulas.description: Cheeger constant as the minimum edge-boundary-to-volume ratio over all non-trivial subsets S.

variables.\\partial S: Edge boundary of S (edges with one endpoint in S, one outside)
variables.S: Non-empty proper subset of vertices V

formulas.description: Cheeger's inequality bounding the spectral gap in terms of the Cheeger constant.

density-of-states.summary: The density of Laplacian eigenvalues per unit eigenvalue interval per unit volume, whose low-energy behavior encodes the spectral dimension.
density-of-states.definition:
The **density of Laplacian eigenvalues** per unit eigenvalue interval per unit volume:

$$\rho(\lambda) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \delta(\lambda - \lambda_i)$$

For large graphs, viewed as a smooth function. The low-energy behavior controls diffusion:

$$\rho(\lambda) \sim \lambda^{d_{\text{spec}}/2 - 1} \quad \text{as } \lambda \to 0^+$$

The **van Hove singularities** at band edges (peaks in DOS) are diagnostic of structural features.

examples.title: DOS for ℤ^d lattice
examples.body: For the integer lattice ℤ^d, the DOS near λ = 0 scales as ρ(λ) ~ λ^{d/2 - 1}, consistent with spectral dimension d_spec = d. Van Hove singularities appear at the band edges of the Brillouin zone.

formulas.description: Density of states as a normalized sum of Dirac deltas at each Laplacian eigenvalue.
Low-energy power-law scaling of the DOS, defining the spectral dimension.

return-probability.summary: The probability that a continuous-time random walk returns to its starting vertex at time t, scaling as t^{-d_spec/2} and defining the spectral dimension.
return-probability.definition:
The **probability that a continuous-time random walk** (with Laplacian generator) **returns to its starting vertex** at time $t$:

$$P_0(t) = \langle v_0 | e^{-t\Delta} | v_0 \rangle = \int_0^\infty \rho(\lambda) e^{-\lambda t} d\lambda$$

Asymptotic scaling:

$$P_0(t) \sim t^{-d_{\text{spec}}/2}$$

defines the **spectral dimension**.

examples.title: Return probability on ℤ^2
examples.body: On the 2D integer lattice, P_0(t) ~ 1/(πt) as t → ∞, consistent with spectral dimension d_spec = 2. The logarithmic correction in 2D is a well-known subtlety.

formulas.expression: P_0(t) = \langle v_0 | e^{-t\Delta} | v_0 \rangle = \int_0^\infty \rho(\lambda) e^{-\lambda t} d\lambda
formulas.description: Return probability as the Laplace transform of the density of states.
Asymptotic power-law decay of return probability, defining the spectral dimension.

lanczos-algorithm.summary: An iterative method for extreme eigenvalues of sparse symmetric matrices, building a Krylov subspace and tridiagonalizing within it.
lanczos-algorithm.definition:
An **iterative method for extreme eigenvalues** of sparse symmetric matrices. Builds a Krylov subspace and tridiagonalizes within it. Extracts the largest and smallest eigenvalues efficiently.

**Key features:**

- Memory: $O(n)$ vectors stored.
- Per-iteration cost: one sparse matrix-vector product.
- Convergence: rapid for **isolated extreme eigenvalues**, slower for clustered.

examples.title: Computing the spectral gap
examples.body: To find λ₁ (the spectral gap) of a large sparse Laplacian, apply Lanczos with a shift-invert transformation near σ = 0. The algorithm converges to the smallest non-zero eigenvalue in O(√(λ₁/λ_max)) iterations.

shift-invert.summary: A spectral transformation M → (M − σI)⁻¹ that maps eigenvalues near a target σ to the largest in absolute value, enabling efficient access to interior eigenvalues.
shift-invert.definition:
A **spectral transformation** giving access to eigenvalues near a target $\sigma$:

$$M \to (M - \sigma I)^{-1}$$

The eigenvalues closest to $\sigma$ become the largest in absolute value, hence amenable to Lanczos/Arnoldi. Requires a sparse linear solver for $(M - \sigma I)x = b$.

examples.title: Finding interior eigenvalues
examples.body: To find Laplacian eigenvalues near λ = 1.5, form (Δ − 1.5·I)⁻¹ and apply Lanczos. Eigenvalues of the transformed matrix are 1/(λᵢ − 1.5), so those closest to 1.5 become largest in magnitude and converge first.

formulas.description: Shift-invert transformation mapping eigenvalues near σ to the largest in absolute value.

kernel-polynomial-method.summary: A matrix-free spectral approximation technique that expands the density of states in Chebyshev polynomials, estimated via stochastic trace estimation.
kernel-polynomial-method.definition:
A **matrix-free spectral approximation** technique. Expands the density of states in **Chebyshev polynomials**:

$$\rho(\lambda) \approx \sum_{k=0}^{K} \mu_k T_k(\lambda)$$

The **Chebyshev moments** $\mu_k = \text{Tr}\, T_k(\Delta)$ are estimated via random-vector trace estimators:

$$\mu_k \approx \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^R v_r^T T_k(\Delta) v_r$$

Cost: $O(nK)$ for $K$ Chebyshev polynomials and $R$ stochastic vectors. **Matrix-free**: only needs to apply $\Delta$ to a vector.

Particularly suited to large-scale DOS estimation on graphs like the pentagonal multi-sheeted adjacency graph.

examples.title: DOS estimation on a large tiling graph
examples.body: For a pentagonal multi-sheeted tiling with n = 10⁶ vertices, full diagonalization is infeasible (O(n³)). KPM with K = 1000 Chebyshev moments and R = 20 random vectors estimates ρ(λ) in O(n·K·R) = O(2×10¹⁰) operations — tractable on modern hardware.

formulas.description: Chebyshev expansion of the density of states.
Stochastic trace estimator for the k-th Chebyshev moment.

variables.T_k(\\Delta): k-th Chebyshev polynomial applied to the Laplacian

aliases: Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind
chebyshev-polynomial.summary: Orthogonal polynomials on [−1, 1] defined by a stable three-term recurrence, used in KPM for their optimal approximation properties and numerical stability.
chebyshev-polynomial.definition:
Orthogonal polynomial family with three-term recurrence:

$$T_0(x) = 1, \quad T_1(x) = x, \quad T_{k+1}(x) = 2x T_k(x) - T_{k-1}(x)$$

Defined on $[-1, 1]$. Used in KPM because:

- Stable three-term recurrence (no exponential growth of round-off).
- Optimal approximation properties for the relevant function spaces.
- Direct matrix-vector implementation via the recurrence.

examples.title: First few Chebyshev polynomials
examples.body:
T_0(x) = 1
T_1(x) = x
T_2(x) = 2x² − 1
T_3(x) = 4x³ − 3x
T_4(x) = 8x⁴ − 8x² + 1

For matrix application: T_k(Δ)v is computed iteratively using the same recurrence with matrix-vector products, never forming T_k(Δ) explicitly.

formulas.description: Three-term recurrence relation defining the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind.

random-walk.summary: A stochastic process stepping uniformly to neighbors on a graph, with the graph Laplacian as its continuous-time generator.
random-walk.definition:
A **stochastic process stepping uniformly to neighbors** on a graph. In discrete time:

$$\text{Pr}[X_{t+1} = u \mid X_t = v] = \frac{1}{\deg(v)} \text{ for } u \sim v$$

In continuous time: a Poisson clock of rate $\deg(v)$ at vertex $v$ triggers a jump to a uniformly random neighbor. Generator is the graph Laplacian (suitably normalized).

examples.title: Random walk on a cycle
examples.body: On a cycle C_n, the random walk steps left or right with equal probability 1/2. The mixing time is O(n²), consistent with spectral gap λ₁ ~ 1/n² and the formula t_mix ~ log(n)/λ₁.

formulas.expression: \text{Pr}[X_{t+1} = u \mid X_t = v] = \frac{1}{\deg(v)} \text{ for } u \sim v
formulas.description: Transition probability of a discrete-time random walk: uniform over neighbors.

variables.X_t: Position of the walk at time t

mixing-time.summary: The time for a random walk to approach its stationary distribution, scaling as log(n)/λ₁ and controlled by the spectral gap.
mixing-time.definition:
The **time for a random walk to approach its stationary distribution**. Typically:

$$t_{\text{mix}} \sim \frac{\log n}{\lambda_1}$$

so spectral gap controls mixing.

For expander graphs, $t_{\text{mix}}$ is $O(\log n)$ — extremely fast. For low-dimensional lattices, $t_{\text{mix}}$ is polynomial in $n$.

examples.title: Expander vs. lattice mixing
examples.body: On a 3-regular expander with λ₁ ≥ 0.1, mixing time is O(log n). On the 2D grid with n vertices, λ₁ ~ 1/n, giving mixing time O(n log n) — much slower.

formulas.description: Mixing time of a random walk as a function of graph size and spectral gap.

diameter.summary: The maximum graph distance between any two vertices, scaling as n^{1/d} for d-dimensional lattices.
diameter.definition:
The **maximum graph distance** between any two vertices:

$$\text{diam}(G) = \max_{u, v} d(u, v)$$

For $\mathbb{Z}^n$ restricted to a ball: $\text{diam} \sim n^{1/d}$. The diameter scales inversely with the effective dimension.

examples.title: Diameter of a hypercube
examples.body: The d-dimensional hypercube Q_d has 2^d vertices and diameter d. Thus diam ~ log₂(n), consistent with the expander-like behavior of hypercubes.

formulas.description: Graph diameter as the maximum shortest-path distance over all vertex pairs.

variables.d(u, v): Shortest-path distance between vertices u and v

girth.summary: The length of the shortest cycle in a graph; large girth is important for proving expansion and Ramanujan properties.
girth.definition: The **length of the shortest cycle**. A graph with no cycles (tree) has $\text{girth} = \infty$. **Large girth** is important for proving expansion / Ramanujan properties.

examples.title: Girth and Ramanujan graphs
examples.body: The Ramanujan graphs constructed by Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak have girth Ω(log n), which is optimal for regular graphs. Large girth prevents short-range correlations that would reduce the spectral gap.

expander-graph.summary: A graph with spectral gap bounded away from 0 as graph size grows, exhibiting rapid random-walk mixing and no small bottlenecks.
expander-graph.definition:
A graph with **spectral gap bounded away from 0** as graph size grows:

$$\lambda_1 \geq c > 0 \quad \text{(uniformly in } n\text{)}$$

Equivalently, a small Cheeger constant. Expanders have:

- Rapid random-walk mixing ($O(\log n)$).
- No small "bottlenecks."
- Good error-correcting code performance.

examples.title: Random regular graphs
examples.body: A random d-regular graph (d ≥ 3) is an expander with high probability. Its spectral gap satisfies λ₁ ≥ d − 2√(d−1) − ε with high probability for large n, approaching the Ramanujan bound.

formulas.description: Defining property of an expander: spectral gap bounded away from zero as graph size grows.

ramanujan-graph.summary: A d-regular graph saturating the Alon–Boppana bound, with all non-trivial adjacency eigenvalues bounded by 2√(d−1) — the optimal expander.
ramanujan-graph.definition:
A graph **saturating the Alon–Boppana bound** on spectral gap:

$$|\lambda_i(A)| \leq 2\sqrt{d-1} \quad \forall \lambda_i \neq \pm d$$

(for $d$-regular Ramanujan graphs). These are the "optimal expanders."

examples.title: Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak construction
examples.body: For primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and q ≡ 1 (mod 4) with p ≠ q, the LPS construction yields (p+1)-regular Ramanujan graphs on q(q²−1)/2 vertices. These achieve the Alon–Boppana bound with equality.

formulas.description: Alon–Boppana bound: all non-trivial adjacency eigenvalues of a d-regular Ramanujan graph are bounded by 2√(d−1).

variables.\\lambda_i(A): i-th eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix A
